analysis.one_liner: Tightens FDA safety rules for food, drugs, devices, and cosmetics, with facility fees, more inspections, and mandatory recall authority.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced by Rep. Dingell with 10 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the House Health Subcommittee for nearly two years until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled how the FDA polices the food, drug, device, and cosmetic supply. Food facilities would have to analyze hazards, write food safety plans, and submit to risk-based inspections at least every four years; the FDA would gain mandatory recall power, broader access to company records, and civil penalties up to $500,000 per violation; the CDC would run an active surveillance system tracking foodborne illness. To pay for it, food facilities, drug and device makers, importers, and cosmetic companies would pay registration fees and bear compliance costs, with waivers and longer deadlines for small businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who get hazard controls, real mandatory recalls instead of voluntary ones, country-of-origin labeling on drugs and carbon monoxide warnings on packaged meat and seafood, broader disease surveillance, and whistleblower protections for employees who report violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who eats food or takes medicine

how_it_helps.text: Food facilities would have to identify hazards, implement preventive controls, keep monitoring records, and file a written food safety plan reviewed during FDA inspections.

The FDA would gain mandatory recall authority over adulterated or misbranded food, plus administrative detention powers and civil penalties of up to $100,000 for individuals and $500,000 for companies per violation.
Every registered food facility would be inspected at least once every four years on a risk-based schedule, with stronger record access for inspectors.
The CDC would set up an active surveillance system to track foodborne illness, and the FDA would get authority to issue subpoenas and protect whistleblowers.
Packaged meat, poultry, and seafood treated with carbon monoxide to keep it looking fresh would carry a consumer warning, and drugs would get country-of-origin labeling.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and processors pay annual registration fees and compliance costs, drug and device makers pay new registration and inspection fees, importers and cosmetic companies face new registration and reporting requirements, and farms and restaurants would for the first time be subject to FDA record-access and traceability rules. Registration fees are waived for small businesses, and small and very small businesses get extra years to comply with the hazard-control rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food processors, drugmakers, importers, cosmetic makers

drawbacks.text: Food facilities would owe an annual registration fee to fund FDA inspections, and facilities that fail inspections would pay reinspection fees, costs likely passed along in food prices.

The bill extends FDA record-access and traceability rules to farms and restaurants for the first time and requires raw agricultural products to identify the grower, lot, and harvest dates, a real paperwork burden for small producers.
The hazard-analysis, preventive-control, and food-safety-plan requirements would impose ongoing compliance costs on every facility, even with phase-ins of two to three years for smaller businesses.
Imported food would need third-party certification to move quickly through customs, adding cost and a new gatekeeping layer to the import process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is familiar: safer food and medicine versus higher compliance costs that reach consumers through prices. The bill is careful with small business — fee waivers, extra compliance time, and Secretary discretion on standards — and its fees are capped at the actual added cost of inspections. The broadest objection is that the traceability and record rules reach all the way down to farms and restaurants, where the paperwork burden is heavy relative to risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee on February 2, 2009, and never moved again before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell of Michigan introduced the bill on January 28, 2009, joined by Reps. Stupak and Pallone.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 2, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no markup, hearing action, or floor vote ever appears in the record.
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican is listed as a sponsor or cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food, drug, device, and cosmetic manufacturers and importers came out ahead: they never faced the registration fees, mandatory hazard controls, expanded inspections, and mandatory recall authority the bill would have imposed. Consumers did not get the new protections.

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Food and Drug Administration Globalization Act of 2009.

for.name: Reps. Bart Stupak and Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Joined Dingell in introducing the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or floor vote; it remained parked in the Health Subcommittee from February 2009 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, so there is no record of where Republicans stood.

industries.note: The bill imposes annual registration fees, mandatory hazard analysis and preventive controls, risk-based inspections, reinspection fees, and mandatory recall exposure. Its compliance costs are what pays for the safety system consumers get.

New registration and inspection fees, country-of-origin labeling, mandatory recall of adulterated drugs, counterfeit-drug penalties, and generic drug application fees to cover pre-approval inspections.
Establishments would have to register, file ingredient statements, report serious adverse events, and adopt good manufacturing practices.

industries.industry: Food importers and foreign food facilities
industries.note: Imports would face certification requirements, denial of entry if a foreign facility refuses an FDA investigation, and destruction of adulterated shipments — but the bill also creates an expedited lane for certified importers.

For the first time, farms and restaurants would fall under FDA record-access and traceability rules, and produce growers would face minimum safety standards. Small-business phase-ins soften but do not remove the burden.

industries.industry: Third-party food auditors and testing laboratories
industries.note: The bill creates an accreditation system for certifying agents and requires food testing to be done only by certified laboratories, making private auditors and labs a permanent part of the food safety system — with conflict-of-interest rules attached.
